stem: A 27-year-old woman is stung on the forearm by a bee. Within 30 minutes the site is red, warm and swollen. She has no fever, wheezing or rash elsewhere, and her blood pressure is normal.
oneliner: 27F + bee sting on forearm + red, warm, swollen within 30 min + afebrile, no systemic signs → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **needs bacteria and hours to days** to build; this swelling appeared in 30 minutes with no fever
whyNot.B: **red streaks running toward lymph nodes** are absent; the reaction stays at the sting site
whyNot.D: **no systemic signs**: no wheeze, no hypotension, no rash elsewhere
whyNot.E: **mononuclear cells, fibrosis and weeks** of time; this began minutes ago

why: **Red, warm swelling within 30 minutes** of a sting, with no fever or systemic signs = **local acute inflammation** (histamine-driven vasodilation and increased permeability).

stem: A 45-year-old man has a red, warm, painful ankle 6 hours after a sprain. Fluid aspirated from the swollen tissue is protein-rich and contains neutrophils.
oneliner: 45M + ankle sprain 6 h ago + red, warm, painful swelling + protein-rich fluid with neutrophils → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **lymphocytes, macrophages and fibrosis over weeks**; this is hours old and neutrophil-rich
whyNot.C: **low-protein fluid** from hydrostatic or oncotic imbalance; this fluid is protein-rich with neutrophils
whyNot.D: **epithelioid macrophages and giant cells** form over weeks; none here
whyNot.E: **fibroblasts and collagen** appear after days; this is the first hours

why: **Hours-old injury** with a **protein-rich exudate full of neutrophils** = **acute inflammation** (increased vascular permeability from mediators such as histamine and bradykinin).

stem: A 58-year-old woman has a firm 1-cm nodule along her abdominal surgical scar 8 months after hernia repair. The nodule is biopsied and the section is viewed under polarized light. The biopsy is shown.
oneliner: 58F + firm nodule at surgical scar 8 mo after hernia repair + [biopsy under polarized light] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **thick, glassy, disorganized collagen bundles** with no giant cells around foreign material
whyNot.B: **non-caseating granulomas without any foreign material**, usually with hilar nodes
whyNot.C: **pus-filled cavity of neutrophils**, not a giant-cell reaction
whyNot.D: **collagen stays inside the scar** and no giant cells or foreign fibers are seen

why: **Multinucleated giant cells around polarizable material** in a nodule at a surgical site = **foreign body granuloma**.

image.prompt: H&E tissue section viewed under partially polarized light showing several large multinucleated giant cells wrapped around brightly birefringent, glowing white fibers (suture material), in a background of fibroblasts and chronic inflammatory cells. No text or labels.

stem: A 36-year-old man has wheezing, hives and a blood pressure of 80/40 mm Hg with pulse 126/min minutes after multiple wasp stings. His temperature is 37.0°C and his neck veins are flat.
oneliner: 36M + multiple wasp stings + wheeze, hives, BP 80/40, HR 126 within minutes + afebrile, flat neck veins → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **fever and an infectious source** over hours; here onset was minutes after stings with normal temperature
whyNot.C: **no blood loss or trauma**; hives and wheeze are not explained by bleeding
whyNot.D: **distended neck veins and pulmonary edema** in pump failure; veins are flat here
whyNot.E: **spinal injury with bradycardia and warm dry skin**; here pulse is fast with hives and wheeze

why: **Minutes after stings: wheeze, hives, hypotension, tachycardia** = **anaphylaxis**.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has sneezing, nasal congestion and watery eyes every spring when grass pollen counts are high. She is afebrile, uses no nasal sprays, and a nasal smear shows many eosinophils.
oneliner: 19F + sneezing, congestion, watery eyes every spring + afebrile, no nasal sprays + eosinophils in nasal smear → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **fever, sore throat and a 7-10 day course**; this recurs every spring without fever
whyNot.B: **no eosinophils; triggered by temperature or odors**, not pollen season
whyNot.C: **eye-only itching and tearing**; here sneezing and congestion dominate
whyNot.E: **needs prolonged topical decongestant use**; she uses no nasal sprays

why: **Seasonal sneezing and congestion with pollen exposure, afebrile, nasal eosinophils** = **allergic rhinitis**.

stem: A 24-year-old man has itchy, red, tearing eyes in both eyes each spring, with clear watery discharge. He has no cold symptoms, sneezing or swollen nodes, and the itch eases with antihistamine eye drops.
oneliner: 24M + itchy, tearing eyes bilaterally each spring + clear discharge, no cold or sneezing + better with antihistamine drops → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **recent cold and a tender preauricular node**; neither is present
whyNot.C: **sneezing and nasal congestion** are the main problem; he has none
whyNot.D: **thick purulent discharge** with crusting; his discharge is clear and watery
whyNot.E: **gritty burning, not seasonal, not itchy**; his itch is seasonal and responds to antihistamines

why: **Seasonal bilateral itchy, tearing eyes that improve with antihistamines** = **allergic conjunctivitis**.

stem: A 40-year-old man received equine antivenom after a snakebite. Nine days later he has fever, an itchy urticarial rash and painful swollen knees and wrists. Serum C3 is low and he has no wheeze or hypotension.
oneliner: 40M + equine antivenom 9 d ago + fever + urticaria + arthralgia + low C3 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **minutes after exposure with wheeze and hypotension**; this began 9 days later with none
whyNot.B: **local necrotic swelling at the injection site** within hours; here the illness is systemic
whyNot.C: **months of drugs such as hydralazine or procainamide, anti-histone antibodies**; this follows a single exposure
whyNot.D: **mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment**; he has an urticarial rash instead

why: **Fever, rash and arthralgia ~1-2 weeks after foreign serum, with low C3** = **serum sickness** (immune-complex deposition).

stem: A 24-year-old woman has had episodes since childhood of nonitchy, nonpitting swelling of the hands and face, and separate attacks of severe abdominal pain with diarrhea. After a dental extraction yesterday, her tongue and lips swelled and her voice became hoarse. She has no hives, takes no medications, and has low C4 and C2.
oneliner: 24F + recurrent nonpitting swelling of hands/face since childhood + abdominal attacks + airway swelling after dental work + no hives + low C4/C2 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **itching, hives and response to antihistamines**; she has no hives and complement is low
whyNot.C: **needs an ACE inhibitor**; she takes no medications
whyNot.D: **no swelling and normal complement**; porphyria gives abdominal pain with neuropsychiatric signs
whyNot.E: **fever and serositis with normal complement**; no recurrent airway swelling

why: **Recurrent nonpitting swelling without hives, abdominal attacks, trauma trigger and low C4/C2** = **hereditary angioedema**.

stem: A 54-year-old man with CD20-positive lymphoma develops fever of 38.9°C, chills and diffuse muscle pain 30 minutes into his first rituximab infusion. He has no hives, lip swelling or wheeze, and his blood pressure is normal.
oneliner: 54M + first rituximab infusion + fever, chills, myalgia at 30 min + no hives, angioedema or wheeze → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **hives, angioedema, wheeze and hypotension**; none present
whyNot.B: **arthralgia, rash and low C3 about 1-2 weeks later**; this is 30 minutes in
whyNot.C: **falling blood pressure and bacteremia**; symptoms started with the infusion and pressure is normal
whyNot.E: **takes 48-72 hours** to appear; this began within an hour

why: **Fever and myalgia during the first anti-CD20 infusion without allergic signs** = **infusion reaction** from cytokines released by lysed B cells.

stem: A 9-month-old boy has had three episodes of otitis media and two of pneumonia since age 6 months, caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. Examination shows no palpable tonsils or cervical lymph nodes. He has had no problems with viral or fungal infections.
oneliner: 9M + recurrent otitis and pneumonia from 6 mo (pneumococcus, Haemophilus) + no tonsils or nodes + no viral/fungal trouble → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **catalase-positive organisms, abscesses and granulomas**; his infections are with encapsulated bacteria
whyNot.B: **hypocalcemia, heart defect and viral/fungal infections**; none described
whyNot.D: **usually mild or silent, and tonsils are present**; this boy has severe pyogenic infections and no tonsils
whyNot.E: **onset in the teens to twenties with normal B-cell numbers**; this started at 6 months

why: **Boy with encapsulated-bacteria infections starting at ~6 months (maternal IgG wanes) and no tonsils** = **Bruton agammaglobulinemia** (Btk defect, no mature B cells).

stem: A 10-month-old boy has recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia and otitis media. Blood counts are normal and HIV testing is negative. Serum IgG is 40 mg/dL (normal 300-1,000 mg/dL for age) with IgA and IgM undetectable. Serum protein electrophoresis shows normal albumin, alpha and beta peaks but no gamma peak.
oneliner: 10M + recurrent pneumococcal infections + normal counts, HIV neg + IgG 40, IgA/IgM undetectable + no gamma peak on SPEP → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **onset in adolescence or adulthood**; this boy is 10 months old
whyNot.B: **normal immunoglobulins and catalase-positive abscesses**; his gamma peak is absent
whyNot.D: **only IgA is low** with a present gamma peak; here all classes are low
whyNot.E: **a sharp monoclonal spike** in older adults; this tracing has no gamma peak at all

why: **Infant boy with pyogenic infections and an absent gamma peak, all immunoglobulin classes low** = **X-linked agammaglobulinemia**.

stem: An 11-month-old boy has had recurrent otitis media and pneumonia since age 7 months. Flow cytometry shows CD3+ T cells at 70% of lymphocytes (normal), CD19+ B cells below 1% (normal about 10-30%), and low serum immunoglobulins.
oneliner: 11M + recurrent otitis/pneumonia since 7 mo + CD3 T cells normal + CD19 B cells <1% + low Ig → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **B cells are present and IgM is high**; here B cells are nearly absent
whyNot.C: **T cells are very low**; his CD3 count is normal
whyNot.D: **B cells and other immunoglobulins are normal**; here B cells are missing and Ig is low
whyNot.E: **B-cell numbers are usually normal and onset is later**; here B cells are absent at 11 months

why: **Normal T cells, near-absent CD19+ B cells, low immunoglobulins in a boy** = **X-linked agammaglobulinemia**.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent sinopulmonary infections and chronic watery diarrhea; stool shows Giardia. Serum IgM is elevated while IgG and IgA are low. B-cell and T-cell counts are normal.
oneliner: 3M + recurrent sinopulmonary infections + chronic Giardia + high IgM, low IgG/IgA + normal B and T counts → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **absent B cells and very low IgM**; his IgM is high
whyNot.B: **IgA alone is low** and IgM is normal; here IgG is low and IgM is high
whyNot.C: **onset in teens or adulthood with low IgM too**; his IgM is elevated
whyNot.D: **profound lymphopenia and early viral/fungal infections**; his B and T counts are normal

why: **High IgM with low IgG and IgA** in a boy with sinopulmonary infections and Giardia = **hyper-IgM syndrome** (failed class switching, usually CD40 ligand deficiency).

stem: A 30-year-old man receives fresh frozen plasma after a car crash. Within 15 minutes he has wheezing, hives and a blood pressure of 80/50 mm Hg. He has no fever or hemoglobinuria, his chest x-ray is clear, and his serum IgG and IgM are normal. He has had mild recurrent sinus infections.
oneliner: 30M + FFP transfusion + wheeze, hives, BP 80/50 within 15 min + no fever, clear CXR + normal IgG/IgM + mild recurrent sinusitis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **all immunoglobulin classes are low**; his IgG and IgM are normal
whyNot.C: **severe pyogenic infections from infancy and low IgG**; his IgG is normal
whyNot.D: **bilateral infiltrates and hypoxemia** within hours; his chest x-ray is clear
whyNot.E: **fever, flank pain and hemoglobinuria** from ABO mismatch; none present

why: **Anaphylaxis to plasma with normal IgG/IgM and mild sinusitis** = **selective IgA deficiency** (anti-IgA antibodies against donor IgA).

stem: A 4-month-old girl has failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, oral thrush and a severe viral pneumonia, after two earlier bacterial infections.
oneliner: 4F + failure to thrive + chronic diarrhea + thrush + severe viral pneumonia + prior bacterial infections → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **catalase-positive bacterial and fungal abscesses without viral susceptibility**; she has severe viral and fungal infections
whyNot.B: **bacterial infections only, starting after ~6 months**; she has viral and fungal disease at 4 months
whyNot.C: **usually mild or silent**; she is severely ill with infections of all types
whyNot.E: **onset in the teens or twenties**; she is 4 months old

why: **Infant with bacterial, viral and fungal infections, diarrhea and failure to thrive** = **SCID** (combined T- and B-cell failure).

stem: A 3-year-old boy underwent ex vivo gene therapy with a retroviral vector in infancy for a severe immunodeficiency; before treatment he had no T cells or NK cells, while B cells were present but nonfunctional. Platelet count is normal and he has no eczema. He now has marked lymphocytosis from a monoclonal T-cell expansion.
oneliner: 3M + retroviral gene therapy for infant immunodeficiency (T-, NK-, B+) + normal platelets, no eczema + now monoclonal T-cell leukemia → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (common gamma chain deficiency)

whyNot.A: **lacks T, B and NK cells** (autosomal recessive); here B cells were present
whyNot.C: **eczema and thrombocytopenia**; his platelets are normal and he has no eczema
whyNot.D: **neutrophil defect with normal T and NK cells**; his T and NK cells were absent
whyNot.E: **T cells are present** and IgM is high; his T cells were absent

answer: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (IL-2 receptor gamma chain)
why: **T-/NK-/B+ boy treated with a retroviral vector who later develops T-cell leukemia** = **X-linked SCID** (insertional mutagenesis).

stem: A 5-month-old girl has severe recurrent infections and a lymphocyte count of 300/µL. Her lymphocytes accumulate dATP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase.
oneliner: 5F + severe recurrent infections + lymphocytes 300/µL + dATP buildup blocking ribonucleotide reductase → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **dGTP (not dATP) builds up and T cells are mainly affected**, often later with neurologic signs
whyNot.B: **boys only, with normal purine metabolites**; she is a girl with dATP excess
whyNot.C: **hypocalcemia and a cardiac defect**; metabolite buildup is not part of it
whyNot.D: **absent HLA-DR**; the problem here is a toxic metabolite

why: **dATP accumulation blocking DNA synthesis in lymphocytes** = **ADA deficiency** (autosomal recessive SCID).

stem: A 7-month-old girl has recurrent pneumonia, otitis media and diarrhea. She has a lymphocyte count of 400/µL, no antibody response to vaccines, no thymic shadow on chest x-ray, and flared costochondral junctions. Her older sister died of infection at 8 months.
oneliner: 7F + recurrent pneumonia, otitis, diarrhea + lymphocytes 400/µL + no vaccine response + no thymic shadow + flared costochondral junctions + sister died → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **X-linked, affecting boys, with normal purine metabolites**; here a girl and her sister are affected
whyNot.C: **neurologic problems** with T cells mainly affected and no rib changes; she has global lymphopenia with flared ribs
whyNot.D: **hypocalcemia, cardiac defect and dysmorphic face**; none described
whyNot.E: **absent HLA-DR with low CD4 only**; she has global lymphopenia and a purine abnormality

why: **SCID picture in a girl with an affected sister** and **flared costochondral junctions** = **ADA deficiency** (autosomal recessive purine salvage defect).

stem: A 3-day-old boy has a seizure with serum calcium 6.1 mg/dL. He has micrognathia and low-set ears, and imaging shows a right-sided aortic arch.
oneliner: 3d M + seizure with Ca 6.1 + micrognathia + low-set ears + right-sided aortic arch → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **malar hypoplasia and ear atresia** without hypocalcemia or arch anomaly
whyNot.B: **cleft palate and tongue falling back** without calcium or cardiovascular disease
whyNot.C: **clenched overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet**; none described
whyNot.E: **hypercalcemia and supravalvular aortic stenosis**; he has hypocalcemia

why: **Hypocalcemia, aortic arch anomaly and facial dysmorphism in a newborn** = **DiGeorge syndrome** (failed third/fourth pharyngeal pouch development).

stem: A 7-month-old girl has Pneumocystis pneumonia, confirmed by a silver stain of lavage fluid, and chronic diarrhea. HIV PCR is negative. CD4+ T cells are low, CD8+ T cells and B-cell counts are normal, and flow cytometry shows no HLA-DR on her B cells and monocytes.
oneliner: 7F + Pneumocystis pneumonia on silver stain + chronic diarrhea + HIV PCR neg + low CD4, normal CD8/B + no HLA-DR → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome type II)

whyNot.A: **global T-cell loss including CD8**; her CD8 and B counts are normal
whyNot.B: **HIV PCR is negative**
whyNot.D: **HLA-DR is present**; the defect is CD40 ligand with high IgM
whyNot.E: **hypocalcemia, heart defect and dysmorphic face**; none described

answer: MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome type II)
why: **Opportunistic infection, low CD4 cells and absent HLA-DR with HIV negative** = **MHC class II deficiency**.

stem: A 10-year-old girl has had chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis with recurrent bacterial respiratory infections since early childhood. Immunoglobulin levels are normal and she has had no opportunistic infections, lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Flow cytometry shows normal B-cell and NK-cell counts but no MHC class I on her lymphocytes.
oneliner: 10F + chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, recurrent bacterial infections + normal Ig + no opportunistic infection or lymphadenopathy + no MHC class I on lymphocytes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **profound lymphopenia and opportunistic infections early in life**; she has neither
whyNot.B: **lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and autoimmune cytopenias**; none present
whyNot.D: **lymphoproliferation, autoimmunity and CMV/EBV problems**; MHC I is lost here
whyNot.E: **absent HLA-DR with PJP and diarrhea**; her defect is class I

answer: Bare lymphocyte syndrome type I (MHC class I deficiency)
why: **Chronic bacterial sinopulmonary disease with absent MHC class I and normal Ig/B/NK** = **bare lymphocyte syndrome type I**.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has eczema, recurrent otitis media, and easy bruising with petechiae; platelets are 40,000/µL and small.
oneliner: 3M + eczema + recurrent otitis + bruising and petechiae + small platelets 40,000/µL → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **infections only, with normal platelets and no eczema**
whyNot.C: **onset in teens or adults without eczema or low platelets**
whyNot.D: **usually mild, with normal platelet count and no eczema**
whyNot.E: **hypocalcemia and cardiac defect, with normal platelets**

why: **Eczema, recurrent infections and small-platelet thrombocytopenia in a boy** = **Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome**.

stem: A 19-year-old man has had eczema since infancy and recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia. He now has a painless neck mass; biopsy shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. His platelet count is 55,000/µL with small platelets, and HIV testing is negative.
oneliner: 19M + lifelong eczema + recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia + B-cell lymphoma + platelets 55,000/µL (small) + HIV neg → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **no eczema or low platelets and later onset**; this man has both
whyNot.B: **infant hypocalcemia and cardiac defect**; neither is described
whyNot.C: **HIV testing is negative**
whyNot.D: **dry eyes and mouth with anti-SSA**; eczema and thrombocytopenia are not features

why: **Eczema, encapsulated-bacteria infections, small-platelet thrombocytopenia and lymphoma** = **Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome**.

stem: A 14-year-old boy has had progressive unsteady gait since age 3 and frequent sinus and lung infections. Small dilated vessels are visible on the whites of both eyes. He has normal stature and no sun sensitivity, and biopsy of a neck mass shows non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
oneliner: 14M + unsteady gait since age 3 + sinopulmonary infections + dilated scleral vessels + lymphoma, normal height, no sun sensitivity → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **cardiomyopathy, scoliosis and GAA repeat expansion**; no telangiectasia or immune defect
whyNot.C: **marked photosensitivity and skin cancers**; he has no sun sensitivity
whyNot.D: **short stature and a sun-sensitive facial rash**; he is of normal height
whyNot.E: **pancytopenia and radial ray defects**; neither described

why: **Childhood cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, sinopulmonary infections and lymphoma** = **ataxia telangiectasia** (defective ATM DNA repair).

stem: A 5-year-old boy has fever, weight loss and enlarged lymph nodes. Culture grows Mycobacterium avium complex. HIV testing is negative, the NBT test is normal and serum interferon-gamma is high. An acid-fast stain of a lymph node biopsy is shown.
oneliner: 5M + fever, weight loss, big nodes + Mycobacterium avium complex + HIV neg, NBT normal, IFN-γ high + [AFB stain of node] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **NBT test is abnormal**; his NBT is normal and mycobacteria are not the typical pathogens
whyNot.B: **neutrophilia, delayed cord separation and pus-free infections**; none described
whyNot.C: **IFN-γ level is low** because IL-12 signaling fails; his IFN-γ is high
whyNot.E: **HIV testing is negative**

why: **Disseminated atypical mycobacteria in a child with high IFN-γ and bacilli-packed histiocytes without granulomas** = **IFN-γ receptor deficiency**.

image.prompt: Lymph node section with acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen) stain showing sheets of pale histiocytes packed with numerous red rod-shaped bacilli, with no organized granulomas, epithelioid cells or giant cells.

stem: A 7-year-old boy has had lymph node and spleen enlargement since infancy, with episodes of autoimmune hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Immunoglobulin levels are normal, ANA is negative, he has had no recurrent infections, and EBV testing is negative. His blood has many CD4-CD8- (double-negative) T cells.
oneliner: 7M + nodes and spleen big since infancy + autoimmune hemolysis and low platelets + normal Ig, ANA neg, EBV neg + many double-negative T cells → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **ANA-positive multisystem disease usually in young women**; his ANA is negative
whyNot.C: **neonatal diarrhea, type 1 diabetes and eczema from FOXP3 loss**; none described
whyNot.D: **acute illness with EBV positivity**; his EBV is negative and the course is chronic
whyNot.E: **low immunoglobulins and recurrent infections**; his immunoglobulins are normal

why: **Chronic nodes and spleen** with **autoimmune cytopenias** and **double-negative T cells** = **ALPS** (defective Fas-mediated apoptosis).

stem: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent abscesses of the skin, lymph nodes and liver. Cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus, Serratia marcescens and Burkholderia cepacia, while streptococcal infections have been rare. His neutrophils ingest bacteria normally but kill catalase-positive species poorly.
oneliner: 3M + recurrent skin, node and liver abscesses + Staph, Serratia, Burkholderia, few strep + normal ingestion but poor killing of catalase-positive bacteria → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **bacteria are killed normally** because H2O2 is still made; infections are mild
whyNot.B: **marked neutrophilia, delayed cord separation and pus-free infections**; none described
whyNot.C: **partial albinism and giant granules**; none described
whyNot.D: **encapsulated-bacteria infections with absent B cells**; his organisms are catalase-positive

why: **Catalase-positive organisms survive while catalase-negative ones are killed** = **CGD**: no NADPH oxidase, so no respiratory burst; catalase-negative bacteria supply their own H2O2.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has had staphylococcal skin abscesses since infancy, vertebral osteomyelitis, and now Aspergillus pneumonia. His platelet count and calcium are normal and he has no rash. The nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) dye stays colorless after neutrophil stimulation.
oneliner: 9M + lifelong staph abscesses + vertebral osteomyelitis + Aspergillus pneumonia + normal platelets and calcium, no rash + NBT test stays colorless → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **hypopigmentation and giant granules** with neutropenia; none described
whyNot.C: **hypocalcemia, heart defect and viral/fungal infections** with normal NBT; his calcium is normal
whyNot.D: **eczema and small-platelet thrombocytopenia**; his platelets are normal with no rash
whyNot.E: **NBT turns blue** and infections are mild; his NBT stays colorless

why: **Staphylococcal and Aspergillus infections with a negative NBT test** = **CGD** (no respiratory burst).

stem: A 2-year-old boy has recurrent Staphylococcus aureus abscesses, a maternal uncle who died of similar infections, and a normal IgE level. Stimulated neutrophils show no oxidative burst on flow cytometry.
oneliner: 2M + recurrent Staph aureus abscesses + maternal uncle died similarly + normal IgE + no neutrophil oxidative burst → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **neutrophilia and pus-free infections with normal burst**; his burst is absent
whyNot.B: **partial albinism and giant granules** with intact burst
whyNot.C: **oxidative burst is present**; infections are milder
whyNot.E: **very high IgE, eczema and retained teeth**; his IgE is normal

why: **X-linked pattern, staphylococcal abscesses and absent respiratory burst** = **CGD**.

stem: A 3-month-old boy had a persistent umbilical cord stump until 5 weeks of age and now has skin ulcers and gingival infections that respond slowly to antibiotics. His white count is 28,000/µL with 80% neutrophils, and biopsy of an infected skin site shows almost no neutrophils in the tissue, with no pus.
oneliner: 3M + late cord separation + skin ulcers and gum infections + WBC 28,000 (80% neutrophils) + no pus at infected sites → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **pus-forming abscesses with catalase-positive organisms**; his tissue has almost no neutrophils
whyNot.B: **partial albinism and giant granules** with neutropenia
whyNot.D: **eczema, very high IgE and cold abscesses**; none described
whyNot.E: **normal neutrophil count and absent B cells**; he has marked neutrophilia

why: **Delayed cord separation, marked neutrophilia and pus-free infections** = **LAD type 1** (CD18 integrin defect stops neutrophils leaving the blood).

stem: A 2-year-old boy has recurrent skin, airway and perirectal infections. White count is 32,000/µL with 85% neutrophils on repeated testing. Neutrophil phagocytosis, bacterial killing and the oxidative burst are normal, but chemotaxis toward C5a is markedly reduced.
oneliner: 2M + recurrent skin, airway, perirectal infections + WBC 32,000 (85% neutrophils) + normal phagocytosis, killing, burst + poor chemotaxis to C5a → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **the oxidative burst is absent**; his burst is normal
whyNot.B: **killing is normal and no neutrophilia**; he has marked neutrophilia and poor chemotaxis
whyNot.D: **neutropenia and giant granules** with partial albinism
whyNot.E: **neutropenia about every 21 days**; his count is persistently high

why: **Persistent neutrophilia with intact burst and killing but failed chemotaxis** = **LAD type 1** (neutrophils cannot adhere and exit vessels).

stem: A 4-year-old girl has silvery hair, light skin and recurrent bacterial skin infections. Her blood smear shows neutropenia with giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils.
oneliner: 4F + silvery hair + light skin + recurrent bacterial infections + neutropenia with giant granules in neutrophils → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **normal pigmentation and normal granules**; the problem is a respiratory burst failure
whyNot.C: **marked neutrophilia, not neutropenia**, and no pigment change
whyNot.D: **infections are mild and neutrophil granules look normal**
whyNot.E: **no immune defect, giant granules or neutropenia**

why: **Partial albinism, recurrent infections and giant neutrophil granules** = **Chediak-Higashi syndrome** (defective lysosomal trafficking).

stem: A 41-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes has recurrent Candida infections of the mouth and vagina. She has a normal neutrophil count. Her neutrophils phagocytose normally and make hydrogen peroxide, and the NBT test is normal, but they cannot produce hypochlorous acid.
oneliner: 41F + diabetes + recurrent oral/vaginal Candida + normal neutrophil count + normal NBT, H2O2 made, no hypochlorous acid → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **NBT is abnormal and H2O2 is not made**; hers is normal
whyNot.B: **partial albinism and giant granules**; none described
whyNot.C: **neutrophilia and impaired chemotaxis**; her count and migration are normal
whyNot.D: **T-cell defect with normal hypochlorite production**; hers is missing

why: **Normal burst and H2O2 but no hypochlorite, with Candida infections** = **myeloperoxidase deficiency**.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is hospitalized for his second episode of meningococcal meningitis and has had no other serious infections. Immunoglobulin levels and neutrophil function are normal.
oneliner: 9M + second meningococcal meningitis + no other serious infections + normal Ig and neutrophil function → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Terminal complement (C5-C9, membrane attack complex) deficiency

whyNot.A: **low IgA with sinopulmonary and GI infections**; his immunoglobulins are normal
whyNot.C: **all immunoglobulins are low** with many pyogenic infections; his are normal
whyNot.D: **abscesses with catalase-positive organisms**; neutrophil function is normal
whyNot.E: **recurrent swelling attacks**, not infections

why: **Recurrent Neisseria infections with normal Ig and phagocytes** = **terminal complement (MAC) deficiency**.

stem: A 22-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, a hot swollen right knee, migratory joint pains and a few pustules on her hands. Gram stain of knee fluid shows gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils, and a cervical culture grows Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Two years ago she had meningococcal meningitis. Total hemolytic complement (CH50) is 5% of normal while C3 and C4 levels are normal. Immunoglobulin levels are normal.
oneliner: 22F + hot knee + migratory arthralgia + pustules + gram-negative diplococci in joint fluid + prior meningococcal meningitis + CH50 5%, C3/C4 normal → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **severe infections with many pyogens and a low C3**; her C3 is normal
whyNot.B: **angioedema attacks and a low C4**; her C4 is normal and infection recurs
whyNot.C: **X-linked in males with a normal CH50**; she is female and her CH50 is very low
whyNot.E: **normal CH50 and immunoglobulins other than IgA**; her CH50 is near zero

answer: Terminal complement deficiency (C5-C9, membrane attack complex)
why: **Recurrent disseminated Neisseria infections with CH50 ~5% and normal C3/C4** = **terminal complement deficiency**.

stem: A 45-year-old man has fatigue and reduced urine output 4 months after a deceased-donor kidney transplant. His creatinine rose from 1.3 to 2.6 mg/dL over a week. Tacrolimus trough is within the target range, he has no fever, and ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis. Biopsy shows lymphocytes invading the tubular epithelium and the walls of small arteries, with no viral inclusions in tubular cells.
oneliner: 45M + 4 mo post kidney transplant + creatinine 1.3 → 2.6 + tacrolimus level in range + biopsy: lymphocytes in tubules and artery walls, no viral inclusions → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis and intimal thickening** over months to years; this shows active lymphocytic invasion
whyNot.C: **vacuolated tubules and arteriolar hyalinosis with high drug levels**; his level is in range
whyNot.D: **minutes to hours after reperfusion** from preformed antibodies; this is 4 months out
whyNot.E: **viral inclusions in tubular cells**; none seen here

why: **Rising creatinine with tubulitis and endarteritis at therapeutic drug levels** = **acute cellular rejection** by host T cells.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with burns receives her first skin graft from an unrelated donor. Ten days later the graft is dusky and sloughing, and biopsy shows a dense lymphocytic infiltrate with no neutrophils or bacteria.
oneliner: 28F + first skin graft from unrelated donor + dusky sloughing graft at day 10 + dense lymphocytes, no neutrophils or bacteria → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **within minutes to hours** from preformed antibodies; this is day 10
whyNot.B: **donor cells attacking the host** in an immunocompromised recipient; here host T cells attack the graft
whyNot.C: **months to years** with fibrosis and vascular narrowing
whyNot.D: **neutrophils and bacteria**; the biopsy shows lymphocytes only

why: **First graft from an unrelated donor failing at ~10 days with lymphocytes** = **acute rejection** (host T-cell response to foreign MHC).

stem: A 42-year-old man with AML develops a maculopapular rash on his palms, watery diarrhea and a bilirubin of 6.2 mg/dL 4 weeks after allogeneic bone marrow transplant. He has no fever and has started no new drugs. Stool cultures and CMV PCR are negative, and his liver is not enlarged or tender and he has no ascites.
oneliner: 42M + allogeneic marrow transplant 4 wk ago + palmar rash + watery diarrhea + bilirubin 6.2 + afebrile, no new drugs, CMV and stool cultures neg, no ascites → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **host T cells attacking the graft, causing marrow failure**, not skin, gut and liver disease
whyNot.C: **CMV PCR is negative**
whyNot.D: **needs a new drug exposure**; he has started none, and drug rashes rarely bring diarrhea and jaundice
whyNot.E: **painful hepatomegaly, ascites and weight gain**; none present, and no rash or diarrhea occurs

why: **Rash, diarrhea and jaundice weeks after marrow transplant** = **acute GVHD** (donor T cells attacking skin, gut and liver).

stem: A 26-year-old woman has 3 months of fatigue and painful swollen wrists and knees, plus painless mouth ulcers. A flat red rash covers her cheeks and nose but spares the nasolabial folds. She had pleuritic chest pain last year, hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL and platelets are 90,000/µL. She has no recent tick bite or genital symptoms.
oneliner: 26F + fatigue + wrist/knee arthritis + painless oral ulcers + malar rash sparing nasolabial folds + prior pleurisy + anemia, low platelets → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **erosive symmetric small-joint disease**; no malar rash, oral ulcers or cytopenias
whyNot.B: **tick bite, erythema migrans and large-joint arthritis**; she has no tick exposure
whyNot.D: **purulent monoarthritis with pustules and genital symptoms**; she has none
whyNot.E: **urethritis, conjunctivitis and enthesitis** after infection; none present

why: **Malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, arthritis, oral ulcers, pleurisy and cytopenias** = **SLE**.

stem: A 23-year-old woman has 2 months of fatigue and morning stiffness in her hands. Serum C3 and C4 are low. A photograph of her face is shown.
oneliner: 23F + fatigue + morning hand stiffness + low C3/C4 + [photo of face] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **no facial rash**; low complement is also not expected
whyNot.B: **violaceous eyelid rash and proximal muscle weakness**; she has hand stiffness only
whyNot.D: **papules and pustules with flushing, involving the nasolabial folds**, with no joint disease or low complement
whyNot.E: **self-limited illness with normal complement**; hers is chronic with low C3/C4

why: **Butterfly rash with hand stiffness and low complement** = **SLE** (type III hypersensitivity, immune-complex consumption of complement).

stem: A 24-year-old woman has 3 months of fatigue, a facial rash, and painful hands and knees. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein and red blood cell casts, and ANA is positive. Her RPR is positive, but the FTA-ABS treponemal test is negative. Monospot, HIV antigen/antibody and hepatitis B surface antigen are all negative.
oneliner: 24F + rash, joint pain, fatigue + proteinuria with RBC casts + ANA positive + RPR positive but FTA-ABS negative + monospot, HIV, HBsAg neg → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **monospot is negative**, and RBC casts are not expected
whyNot.C: **HIV antigen/antibody is negative**
whyNot.D: **HBsAg is negative**
whyNot.E: **the treponemal FTA-ABS is negative**, so the RPR is a false positive

why: **Facial rash, arthritis and RBC casts** with a **biologic false-positive RPR** (antiphospholipid antibodies) = **SLE with lupus nephritis**.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has a butterfly-shaped facial rash and joint pain. Her 24-hour urine protein is 2 g with microscopic hematuria, and anti-nucleosome antibodies are positive.
oneliner: 33F + butterfly facial rash + joint pain + proteinuria 2 g/day + hematuria + anti-nucleosome antibodies → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **symmetric erosive joint disease** without a malar rash or glomerulonephritis
whyNot.B: **proximal weakness and violaceous eyelid rash**; neither described
whyNot.C: **tight skin and Raynaud phenomenon**; neither described
whyNot.D: **dry eyes and mouth**; no facial rash or nephritis

why: **Malar rash, arthralgia, nephritis and anti-nucleosome antibodies** = **SLE**.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has had Raynaud phenomenon for years, with swollen fingers, tight shiny facial skin with a puckered mouth, heartburn and difficulty swallowing solids. Her blood pressure is now 175/105 mm Hg.
oneliner: 45F + Raynaud for years + swollen fingers + tight shiny facial skin, puckered mouth + heartburn and dysphagia + BP 175/105 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **high-titer anti-U1 RNP with overlap features** such as arthritis or myositis; none described
whyNot.C: **malar rash, oral ulcers and arthritis**; none described, and tight skin is not typical
whyNot.D: **proximal weakness and violaceous rash**; none described
whyNot.E: **dry eyes and mouth**, not skin thickening and sclerosis

why: **Raynaud, tight facial skin, esophageal dysmotility and new hypertension** = **systemic sclerosis**.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has had cold-induced color changes in her fingers for 2 years, with painful fingertip ulcers and heartburn. Over the past year her forearm and trunk skin has thickened. For 6 months she has had progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. Bibasilar fine crackles are heard, FVC is 58% of predicted and DLCO is reduced. A skin biopsy shows thickened dermis with dense collagen and loss of skin appendages.
oneliner: 52F + 2 y Raynaud with digital ulcers + heartburn + skin thickening of forearms and trunk + 6 mo dyspnea and dry cough + low FVC, DLCO + biopsy: dense dermal collagen, lost appendages → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **lung disease without skin thickening, Raynaud or digital ulcers**
whyNot.B: **hilar adenopathy and non-caseating granulomas**; skin shows dense collagen instead
whyNot.C: **malar rash, oral ulcers and serositis**; skin is thickened, not rashy
whyNot.E: **proximal weakness and heliotrope rash**; she has none

why: **Raynaud, digital ulcers, skin thickening with dermal collagen, reflux and lung fibrosis** = **systemic sclerosis**.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has had tight skin on her fingers, upper arms and trunk and cold-induced hand pain for 8 months. She now presents with a severe headache. Her blood pressure is 210/120 mm Hg and creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL. Serum anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibody is positive.
oneliner: 48F + 8 mo tight skin of fingers, upper arms and trunk + cold-induced hand pain + severe headache, BP 210/120, creatinine 0.9 → 2.4 + anti-Scl-70 positive → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **anti-centromere, skin limited to the face and below the elbows** and rare renal crisis; hers reaches the upper arms and trunk with anti-Scl-70
whyNot.C: **proximal weakness and heliotrope rash** with anti-Jo-1 or Mi-2
whyNot.D: **malar rash, anti-dsDNA and active urine sediment**; none described
whyNot.E: **high anti-U1 RNP titers and overlap features**; hers is anti-Scl-70

why: **Anti-topoisomerase I**, **skin thickening of the upper arms and trunk** and a **hypertensive renal crisis** = **diffuse systemic sclerosis**.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has 2 years of dry mouth, gritty eyes and painless bilateral parotid enlargement. ANA and anti-SSA (Ro) are positive.
oneliner: 52F + 2 y dry mouth + gritty eyes + painless parotid enlargement + ANA and anti-SSA positive → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **granulomatous parotid disease with hilar nodes**; anti-SSA and keratoconjunctivitis sicca point elsewhere
whyNot.B: **acute tender swelling with fever** that settles in days; hers is chronic and painless
whyNot.C: **joint disease and rheumatoid factor** leading the picture; sicca with anti-SSA is her main problem
whyNot.D: **malar rash, nephritis and anti-dsDNA**; her main problem is sicca symptoms

why: **Dry eyes, dry mouth, enlarged salivary glands and anti-SSA/Ro** = **Sjogren syndrome**.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has 2 months of trouble climbing stairs and lifting her arms to comb her hair. Creatine kinase is 2,400 U/L and urinalysis is normal. A photograph of her face and hands is shown.
oneliner: 44F + 2 mo trouble climbing stairs and combing hair + CK 2,400, normal urinalysis + [photo of face and hands] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **no skin lesions** in polymyositis; she has a violaceous eyelid and knuckle rash
whyNot.C: **malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds and arthritis**, with normal CK
whyNot.D: **silvery plaques with nail pitting** and no weakness
whyNot.E: **periorbital edema from proteinuria**; her urinalysis is normal and she has weakness with high CK

why: **Proximal weakness with raised CK, violaceous eyelids and scaly knuckle papules** = **dermatomyositis**.

image.prompt: Composite clinical photograph: on the left, a woman's eyelids with a violet-purple discoloration and mild swelling of the upper lids; on the right, the back of her hand with flat-topped, scaly, violaceous papules over the knuckles. No text or labels.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with SLE, gravida 4 para 0030, has had three miscarriages, each at about 10 weeks. Her lupus is quiet, with normal complement and no rash or joint symptoms. She has never had a blood clot.
oneliner: 29F + SLE + G4P0030, three miscarriages at ~10 wk + quiet lupus, normal complement + no clots → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **rash, arthritis, nephritis and low complement**; none present now
whyNot.B: **venous clots from activated protein C resistance**; she has had none
whyNot.C: **venous thrombosis and skin necrosis** with warfarin; no clots here
whyNot.E: **venous clotting without lupus association**; no clots here

why: **Lupus with recurrent pregnancy loss and quiet disease** = **antiphospholipid syndrome**.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has a painful swollen left leg; Doppler ultrasound shows a deep vein thrombosis. She had a fetal death at 20 weeks last year. Platelets are 110,000/µL, PT is normal, and the aPTT is prolonged and does not correct on mixing with normal plasma.
oneliner: 27F + DVT + fetal death at 20 wk + platelets 110,000 + normal PT + long aPTT not corrected by mixing → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **normal aPTT** with activated protein C resistance; hers is prolonged and uncorrected
whyNot.B: **normal aPTT**; no inhibitor effect on clotting tests
whyNot.D: **normal aPTT**; the prothrombin gene mutation does not prolong it
whyNot.E: **normal aPTT**; protein S loss does not prolong it

why: **Venous clot plus fetal loss with a long aPTT that does not correct** = **antiphospholipid syndrome** (lupus anticoagulant).

stem: A 34-year-old woman has 2 months of fatigue, constipation and frequent urination, without fever or weight loss. Serum calcium is 12.6 mg/dL, PTH is low and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is high. Chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar enlargement.
oneliner: 34F + fatigue, constipation, polyuria + Ca 12.6, low PTH, high 1,25-vitamin D + bilateral hilar enlargement + no fever or weight loss → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **PTH is high** in primary hyperparathyroidism; hers is suppressed
whyNot.B: **fever, night sweats and weight loss**; she has none
whyNot.D: **fever, night sweats and cough with caseation**; she has no constitutional symptoms
whyNot.E: **low 1,25-vitamin D with a mass and weight loss**; hers is high with symmetric nodes

why: **Hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH, high calcitriol and bilateral hilar nodes** = **sarcoidosis** (macrophage 1-alpha hydroxylase).

stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C has fatigue, joint pains, a rash on his legs and an enlarged spleen. Platelet count is normal, serum rheumatoid factor is positive and C4 is low. A photograph of his legs is shown.
oneliner: 52M + chronic hepatitis C + fatigue + arthralgia + splenomegaly + normal platelets, RF positive, low C4 + [photo of legs] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **hypertension, abdominal pain and normal complement** in medium-vessel disease; low C4 and RF point elsewhere
whyNot.C: **symmetric erosive joint disease** with no purpuric rash and normal complement
whyNot.D: **usually a child with abdominal pain and IgA deposits**; he has low C4 and positive RF
whyNot.E: **non-palpable purpura with low platelets**; his platelets are normal

why: **Hepatitis C with palpable purpura, arthralgia, positive RF and low C4** = **mixed cryoglobulinemia** (immune-complex vasculitis).

image.prompt: Photograph of the lower legs of an adult man showing multiple raised, non-blanching, red-purple palpable purpuric spots of varying size clustered on the shins and ankles. No text or labels.

stem: A 46-year-old man has 3 months of sinusitis with nosebleeds and nasal crusting, then a cough with a lung nodule on chest x-ray, and a week of hematuria. Creatinine is 2.8 mg/dL and cytoplasmic ANCA is positive. Anti-GBM antibodies are negative, eosinophils are normal and he has no asthma.
oneliner: 46M + 3 mo sinusitis with epistaxis + lung nodule + hematuria, creatinine 2.8 + c-ANCA positive + anti-GBM neg, normal eosinophils, no asthma → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **asthma, eosinophilia and p-ANCA**; he has none
whyNot.B: **p-ANCA without sinus disease or lung nodules**; his c-ANCA with sinus disease fits GPA
whyNot.C: **anti-GBM positive with hemoptysis and no sinus disease**; his anti-GBM is negative
whyNot.D: **ANCA is negative in this EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferation**; his c-ANCA is positive with glomerulonephritis

why: **Upper airway disease, lung nodule and glomerulonephritis with c-ANCA** = **GPA**.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has palpable purpura on his legs and buttocks, colicky abdominal pain and hematuria 2 weeks after a sore throat. His platelet count is 310,000/µL.
oneliner: 6M + palpable purpura on legs/buttocks + colicky abdominal pain + hematuria + sore throat 2 wk ago + normal platelets → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **kidney-only hematuria** without purpura or abdominal pain
whyNot.C: **nephrotic-range proteinuria with edema** and no purpura
whyNot.D: **non-palpable petechiae with low platelets**; his platelets are normal and he has abdominal pain and hematuria
whyNot.E: **fever, conjunctivitis and red cracked lips**; none described

why: **Palpable purpura on legs and buttocks, abdominal pain and hematuria with normal platelets** = **IgA vasculitis**.

stem: A 41-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever, weight loss, aching weak muscles and cramping abdominal pain after meals. Blood pressure is 168/102 mm Hg. He has no cough, sinus disease, asthma or hematuria, and ANCA is negative.
oneliner: 41M + 3 wk fever, weight loss, myalgia + post-meal abdominal pain + new BP 168/102 + no cough, sinus disease, asthma or hematuria + ANCA neg → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **sinus, lung and glomerular disease with c-ANCA**; none present
whyNot.B: **asthma and eosinophilia**; he has no asthma
whyNot.C: **young woman with arm pulse deficits and arm BP differences**; he has none
whyNot.E: **age over 50 with headache and jaw claudication**; he has neither

why: **Fever, abdominal pain, myalgia and new hypertension with negative ANCA and no lung or kidney sediment** = **polyarteritis nodosa** (medium-vessel vasculitis).
